questions.stem: Behavioural economics is best described as the study of:
options: how psychological, social and emotional factors affect economic decisions
how governments use taxation and spending to manage the economy as a whole
how consumers always make fully rational and well-informed economic choices
how firms set the prices of their products in order to maximise their profits
questions.explanation: Behavioural economics draws on psychology to explain why people's decisions often depart from the rational choices traditional theory predicts. It does not assume people are fully rational; that is the assumption it tests.

questions.stem: Bounded rationality refers to the idea that:
options: people always weigh every one of the available options fully before choosing the best
people often lack the self-control to act on the long-term plans that they make
people care about fairness and the wellbeing of others as well as about themselves
people's decisions are limited by the information, time and mental capacity they have
questions.explanation: Bounded rationality means people try to choose well but cannot gather and process all relevant information, so they rely on shortcuts. A lack of self-control is bounded willpower, and caring about others is bounded self-interest.

questions.stem: Bounded willpower refers to:
options: people being limited in their choices by the size of the incomes they earn
people choosing short-term gratification over their long-term interests
people being limited by how much information they are able to process
people caring about the wellbeing of others as well as their own wellbeing
questions.explanation: Bounded willpower describes knowing what is best in the long run but giving in to immediate temptation, such as spending instead of saving. Limits on processing information are bounded rationality.

questions.stem: Bounded self-interest refers to people:
options: being willing to give up some of their own gain to help others or to punish unfairness
always acting to maximise their own utility, regardless of the effect on other people
being unable to process all of the information available to them when making choices
putting off saving for the future, even when they have firmly planned to save money
questions.explanation: Bounded self-interest recognises that people care about others and about fairness, so they donate, volunteer or reject unfair deals. Acting purely for oneself regardless of others is the traditional assumption that this insight qualifies.

questions.stem: Liam plans to start a fitness program every Monday, but each week he puts it off until the next. This best illustrates:
options: bounded self-interest
the endowment effect
bounded willpower
bounded rationality
questions.explanation: Liam knows what he wants to do in the long run but keeps choosing the more pleasant option now, which is bounded willpower. He is not short of information about the program, so bounded rationality does not explain his delay.

questions.stem: Sophie donates $50 a month to a charity, although she receives nothing in return. This is best explained by:
options: loss aversion
bounded self-interest
bounded willpower
bounded rationality
questions.explanation: Giving up her own income to help others shows that Sophie's self-interest is bounded by concern for others. Traditional theory, which assumes pure self-interest, struggles to explain gifts that bring the giver no material return.

questions.stem: Choosing a phone plan, Kai faces 40 options and simply picks the one his friend uses. This is an example of:
options: showing bounded self-interest by helping out his friend
rational choice after weighing every plan's costs fully
using a rule of thumb because of bounded rationality
acting with bounded willpower by choosing very quickly
questions.explanation: Faced with too many options to compare, Kai uses a shortcut, or heuristic, which is a response to bounded rationality. He does not weigh every plan's costs, so this is not the fully rational choice of traditional theory.

questions.stem: Under bounded rationality, people often 'satisfice'. This means that they:
options: refuse to choose at all until every piece of information is freely available
choose the first option that is good enough rather than searching for the best
choose whatever option gives the people around them the greatest satisfaction
keep searching until they are certain they have found the best option available
questions.explanation: Satisficing means settling for an acceptable option because searching for the best one takes time and effort people do not have. Searching until certain of the best is what a fully rational decision-maker would do.

questions.stem: A supermarket finds that when it displays 24 varieties of jam, fewer shoppers buy any jam than when it displays 6. This illustrates:
options: choice overload, a consequence of bounded rationality
the law of demand, as greater variety raises prices
bounded self-interest, as shoppers leave jam for others
the endowment effect, as shoppers value their own jam
questions.explanation: Too many options make comparison hard, so some people avoid choosing at all, which is choice overload. Traditional theory predicts that more choice can only help a rational consumer, because it is easier to find an option that suits them.

questions.stem: A jacket is labelled 'Was $400, now $199'. Shoppers judge $199 a bargain, although similar jackets sell for $150 elsewhere. This illustrates:
options: bounded self-interest
anchoring
loss aversion
the sunk cost fallacy
questions.explanation: The 'was' price acts as an anchor, a reference point that shapes how the sale price is judged. Loss aversion concerns weighing losses more heavily than gains, not the starting figure a judgement is built on.

questions.stem: Shoppers are more likely to buy mince labelled '90% fat-free' than mince labelled '10% fat', although the two are identical. This is:
options: the decoy effect
herd behaviour
the framing effect
the anchoring effect
questions.explanation: Presenting the same information in a positive or negative way changes choices, which is framing. A decoy is an extra, inferior option added to steer choice, and none is offered here.

questions.stem: Loss aversion is the tendency for people to:
options: avoid every purchase that carries even a small risk of losing money
value a gain more highly than they value a loss of exactly the same amount
keep spending on a project because of the money already spent on it
feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain
questions.explanation: People typically weigh a loss more heavily than a gain of the same size, so they work harder to avoid losses than to secure gains. Continuing to spend because of past spending is the sunk cost fallacy, a different bias.

questions.stem: In a classroom experiment, half the students are given a coffee mug. Those with mugs ask far more to sell one than those without will pay to buy one. This result:
options: supports traditional theory, which predicts that owners value goods more
shows bounded self-interest, as owners want to keep the mugs for others
shows the decoy effect, as owners compare their mug with other goods
supports the endowment effect, contradicting the traditional prediction
questions.explanation: Traditional theory predicts that randomly chosen owners and non-owners should value an identical mug about the same. Owners valuing it more simply because they own it is the endowment effect, an insight linked to loss aversion.

questions.stem: In the ultimatum game, a proposer offers a responder a share of $100. If the responder rejects the offer, both receive nothing. Traditional theory predicts that the responder will:
options: accept only offers of at least half, in order to maximise her utility
reject every offer made, in order to punish the proposer for greed
accept any offer above zero, since something is better than nothing
reject any offer below half, since an unequal split of $100 is unfair
questions.explanation: A rational, self-interested responder gains from any positive amount and loses everything by rejecting, so traditional theory predicts acceptance of even $1. Rejecting offers as unfair is what experiments often find, and is explained by bounded self-interest.

questions.stem: In ultimatum game experiments, responders often reject low offers such as $10 of $100. Behavioural economists explain this mainly by:
options: traditional theory: rejecting maximises the money responders receive
bounded self-interest: people will give up money to punish unfairness
bounded rationality: responders miscalculate which choice pays more
bounded willpower: responders cannot resist taking the money at once
questions.explanation: Responders know that rejecting leaves them with nothing, yet many sacrifice the money to punish what they see as an unfair split. This concern with fairness is bounded self-interest. Rejection earns $0, so it cannot maximise money received.

questions.stem: Ava paid $80 for a concert ticket. On the night she feels ill and would rather stay home, but she goes anyway 'so the money isn't wasted'. This illustrates:
options: the sunk cost fallacy
the framing effect
bounded self-interest
anchoring
questions.explanation: The $80 is spent whether or not she goes, so a rational choice would compare only the future costs and benefits of going. Letting a past, unrecoverable cost drive the decision is the sunk cost fallacy.

questions.stem: Noah keeps $2,000 in a holiday savings account earning 1% interest while owing $2,000 on a credit card charging 20%. This is best explained by:
options: rational choice, as Noah earns interest on his savings
mental accounting, treating money differently by its purpose
loss aversion, as Noah fears losing his credit card account
bounded self-interest, as Noah is saving for others' benefit
questions.explanation: Paying off the card would save far more interest than the savings earn, so a rational saver would use the $2,000 to clear the debt. Labelling money for a purpose and refusing to move it is mental accounting.

questions.stem: Offered $100 today or $110 in a week, many people take $100 now. Offered $100 in 52 weeks or $110 in 53 weeks, most choose to wait. This inconsistency is called:
options: anchoring, a form of bounded rationality
fairness, a form of bounded self-interest
present bias, a form of bounded willpower
loss aversion, a form of bounded rationality
questions.explanation: The trade-off is the same one-week wait for $10 in both cases, yet people are impatient only when the reward is immediate. Overweighting the present in this way is present bias, a source of bounded willpower.

questions.stem: Diners choose the busier of two restaurants, assuming the crowd knows which is better. This is an example of:
options: present bias
herd behaviour
loss aversion
the endowment effect
questions.explanation: Following what others do, on the assumption that they know best, is herd behaviour. It is a shortcut people take when they lack information, a form of bounded rationality.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures a key difference between traditional and behavioural economics?
options: Traditional economics uses models; behavioural economics rejects the use of every economic model
Traditional economics assumes irrational choice; behavioural economics assumes fully rational choice
Traditional economics assumes rational choice; behavioural economics finds predictable departures from it
Traditional economics studies consumers; behavioural economics studies only the decisions of governments
questions.explanation: Traditional economics models people as rational, self-interested utility maximisers. Behavioural economics finds systematic, predictable departures from that model. It studies consumers, businesses and governments, and builds its own models rather than rejecting modelling.

questions.stem: Behavioural economics is said to complement, rather than replace, traditional economics. This is because it:
options: applies only to government decisions, leaving consumers to traditional theory
accepts every assumption of traditional theory but tests them with new data
explains departures from rational behaviour while accepting that incentives still matter
shows that traditional economic models cannot make any accurate predictions at all
questions.explanation: Prices, taxes and subsidies still change behaviour much as traditional theory predicts; behavioural economics adds explanations for where people depart from it. It questions assumptions such as full rationality, so it does not accept every traditional assumption.

questions.stem: In behavioural economics, a 'nudge' is:
options: a tax that raises the price of a harmful good in order to reduce its use
a law that bans a harmful product from being sold or advertised at all
a subsidy that lowers the price of a healthy good in order to raise its use
a change in how choices are framed that steers behaviour without limiting options
questions.explanation: A nudge changes the way a choice is presented, such as the default or the order of options, while leaving every option available at the same price. Taxes, bans and subsidies change incentives or rules, which are traditional policy tools.

questions.stem: A school canteen places fruit at eye level beside the till and moves chips to a low shelf, while selling both at the same prices. This is an example of:
options: choice architecture used as a nudge
a regulation that bans unhealthy food
a subsidy that makes healthy food cheaper
price discrimination between students
questions.explanation: Arranging how options are presented to steer choices, without changing prices or removing options, is choice architecture. Chips are still sold at the same price, so there is no ban and no subsidy.

questions.stem: A country moves from an opt-in to an opt-out organ donor register. Behavioural economists expect the number of registered donors to rise, mainly because of:
options: the default effect, as many people stay with the pre-selected option
loss aversion, as people fear losing the chance to help someone in need
anchoring, as the register sets a target number of donors to reach
a tax incentive given to people who agree to become organ donors
questions.explanation: Many people stick with whatever option is pre-selected, through inertia or because they read it as a recommendation, so changing the default changes outcomes. No financial incentive is involved; only the presentation of the choice has changed.

questions.stem: A tax office sends late payers a letter saying that nine out of ten people in their town pay their tax on time. This strategy draws mainly on:
options: social norms, as people tend to follow what most others do
loss aversion, as people fear losing their tax refunds
the endowment effect, as people value their own money more
bounded self-interest, as late payers want to help others
questions.explanation: Telling people that most others pay on time uses the pull of social norms, the tendency to conform to what peers do. The letter offers no new penalty or reward, so loss of a refund is not the lever being used.

questions.stem: Graphic health warnings on cigarette packs aim partly to make the future health costs of smoking more vivid. This targets:
options: anchoring, which leads smokers to rely on the first price
herd behaviour, which leads smokers to follow celebrities
present bias, which leads smokers to discount future costs
loss aversion, which leads smokers to fear wasting money
questions.explanation: Smokers with present bias give too little weight to harms that arrive years later; vivid images make those future costs feel immediate. The warnings do not change the price of cigarettes, so they are not working through prices or money.

questions.stem: A government wants to find out whether an energy-saving message on household bills reduced electricity use. Which approach gives the strongest evidence?
options: survey the households that received the message about whether they liked its design
compare the electricity used by all households this year with usage ten years ago
count how many of the households that received the message said they read it
compare usage of randomly chosen households that got the message with others that did not
questions.explanation: A randomised controlled trial isolates the effect of the message, because the two groups differ only in whether they received it. A ten-year comparison mixes the message's effect with every other change over that time, such as new appliances and prices.

questions.stem: Which is a common criticism of government nudges?
options: they remove consumer choice by banning harmful products outright from sale
they always cost more to run than taxes and regulations designed to do the same job
they work only on the behaviour of businesses and not on the behaviour of consumers
their effects can be small or fade over time, so they may not solve major problems
questions.explanation: Many nudges are cheap, but their effects are often modest and can wear off, so on their own they may not be enough for large problems such as obesity. Nudges keep all options available, so banning products is the opposite of a nudge.

questions.stem: Which government policy relies most on traditional economics rather than behavioural insights?
options: a tax on sugary drinks that raises their price
default enrolment in a savings scheme, with an opt-out
a letter comparing a household's energy use with its neighbours'
placing healthy foods at eye level in public hospitals
questions.explanation: A tax works by changing the price, an incentive that a rational consumer responds to, which is the traditional approach. Defaults, social comparisons and choice architecture all work by changing how choices are presented, drawing on behavioural insights.

questions.stem: Health star ratings on packaged food mainly help consumers who face:
options: price discrimination, by showing which of the foods cost less
bounded rationality, by simplifying complex nutrition information
bounded self-interest, by encouraging them to buy food for others
bounded willpower, by banning unhealthy foods from supermarkets
questions.explanation: Comparing nutrition panels takes time and knowledge that shoppers often lack, so a simple star rating gives them a shortcut, easing bounded rationality. The ratings ban nothing, so they cannot act by removing unhealthy options.

questions.stem: A store's app warns: 'You will lose your 500 reward points if you don't shop by Friday.' This draws mainly on:
options: the decoy effect
anchoring
bounded self-interest
loss aversion
questions.explanation: Framing the offer as avoiding a loss of points, rather than earning a gain, uses loss aversion: people act harder to avoid losing something they already hold. No inferior option or reference price is offered, so it is neither a decoy nor an anchor.

questions.stem: A cinema sells a small popcorn for $5, a medium for $8.50 and a large for $9. Most buyers choose the large. The medium size is acting as:
options: a sunk cost that buyers then try hard to recover
a decoy that makes the large look like good value
an anchor that makes the small look too expensive
a default that most buyers accept without thinking
questions.explanation: Few people want the medium, but it makes the large seem a bargain at only 50 cents more, which is the decoy effect. It does not make the small look expensive; buyers move up to the large, not away from the small.

questions.stem: A hotel booking website shows 'Only 2 rooms left — 14 people are looking at this hotel'. This strategy mainly exploits:
options: scarcity and herd behaviour, pushing buyers to decide quickly
bounded self-interest, encouraging generosity towards the hotel
the endowment effect, by giving free rooms to some of its users
the decoy effect, by adding a deliberately unattractive room
questions.explanation: Signals that a good is scarce and that many others want it create urgency, so buyers decide quickly instead of comparing options. No inferior option is shown and nothing is given away, so neither the decoy nor the endowment effect applies.

questions.stem: A ticket website shows a low headline price, then adds booking and card fees only at the final step of checkout. This 'drip pricing' draws on:
options: anchoring on the headline price and reluctance to abandon effort already spent
bounded self-interest, as buyers want the ticket seller to earn a fair profit
rational choice, as buyers compare the total price at every step of checkout
the decoy effect, as an inferior ticket is added to make others look better
questions.explanation: The low first price anchors buyers' sense of the cost, and having invested time in checkout they are reluctant to start again elsewhere. A fully rational buyer would compare total prices across sellers, which drip pricing makes harder.

questions.stem: A streaming service turns free trials into paid subscriptions automatically unless customers cancel. Many keep paying for a service they rarely use. This works mainly through:
options: the decoy effect on subscription prices
rational utility maximisation by viewers
inertia and the power of defaults
bounded self-interest towards the business
questions.explanation: Continuing is the default, and many people never get around to cancelling, so they keep paying. Rational consumers would cancel once the value of the service fell below its price, which these customers fail to do.

questions.stem: Many retailers price goods at $9.99 rather than $10.00. Behavioural economists explain this mainly by:
options: loss aversion, as shoppers fear losing one cent
bounded self-interest, as shoppers donate their change
shoppers judging a price largely by its first digit
shoppers preferring to receive a coin in change
questions.explanation: Shoppers tend to read $9.99 as 'nine dollars something', so it feels much cheaper than $10.00 although the difference is one cent. This shortcut in processing prices is a form of bounded rationality.

questions.stem: A gym finds that most members who sign 12-month contracts attend far less often than they predicted when they joined. This best supports the idea that:
options: people value the gym more once they hold a membership, a sign of loss aversion
people are fully rational, as each chose the contract that best suited them
people join gyms mainly to help other members, a sign of bounded self-interest
people overestimate their future self-control, a sign of bounded willpower
questions.explanation: Members expected to attend often, but present bias led them to skip sessions when the time came, so they overpaid for a contract they underused. A fully rational member would predict their own attendance accurately and choose a cheaper pay-per-visit option.

questions.stem: In an experiment, students estimate the number of jelly beans in a jar after first being asked whether it holds more or less than 200, or more or less than 2,000. Those given 2,000 estimate much higher. This tests:
options: loss aversion
the endowment effect
bounded self-interest
anchoring
questions.explanation: The number in the first question serves as a reference point that pulls later estimates towards it, which is anchoring. The students own nothing and lose nothing, so the endowment effect and loss aversion are not involved.

questions.stem: Mei knows that saving for retirement matters and has worked out how much she should save, but each week she spends the money on takeaway meals instead. Her behaviour shows:
options: bounded willpower rather than bounded rationality
bounded rationality rather than bounded willpower
bounded self-interest rather than bounded willpower
rational utility maximisation over her whole lifetime
questions.explanation: Mei has the information and has done the calculation, so a lack of information or processing ability is not her problem. Her difficulty is self-control, choosing present enjoyment over her own long-term plan, which is bounded willpower.
